To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
M1 and M3 receptors are present in the airways, and that M1 receptors may play a role in the regulation of airway smooth muscle tone.

M2 receptors inhibit cholinergic neurotransmission in airways, M3 receptors are responsible for the contractile response of airway smooth muscle and the secretion of mucus, and M2 and M3 receptor antagonists may be useful in the treatment of airway hyperresponsiveness and asthma, respectively.
M1 receptors are located on ganglionic parasympathic neurons, M2 receptors are located on nerve endings, and M3 receptors are located on effector organs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of muscarinic receptor sub-types in lung tissue and their role in the regulation of lung function.
the characterization of muscarinic receptor subpopulations in airways and parenchyma and the role of each subtype in the regulation of airway function.
the identification of muscarinic receptor subpopulations in lung and the elucidation of their functional roles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the M3 receptor subtype is the most abundant subtype present in the lung and is the one that is responsible for mediating the bronchoconstrictor effects of acetylcholine.
the muscarinic receptors in airways are predominantly of the M3 subtype, but that the M2 receptor subtype is present in the lung and may play a role in the control of airway tone.
muscarinic receptors in the lung are heterogeneous and that the subtypes may be located on different types of cells and may mediate a variety of effects in the airways.

the airways and parenchyma contain muscarinic receptors that are functionally heterogeneous.
M3 receptors are the major functional receptors mediating the effects of muscarinic agonists in the airways.
the M2 receptors in the airways are primarily autoreceptors and M3 receptors mediate smooth muscle contraction.

muscarinic receptor subtyping in human airways is possible, and that the M1 and M3 receptor subtypes may play important roles in the pathophysiology of asthma.
muscarinic receptor subpopulations are differentially distributed in the lung, and that the M3 receptor is the most important subtype mediating airway smooth muscle contraction.
